import StorageDiagram from "@site/src/components/StorageStrategies";

How experienced teams lay out contract state on Stellar — from your first counter to protocol-scale data layouts. Eleven strategies, ordered simplest to most complex, distilled from a survey of 874 contract files across 493 public repositories.

{/* section:part0 */}

## Why storage is the hard part

On Soroban, contract state is not a big free-form database. It is a set of **ledger entries** — independent key→value pairs. Keys and values can be any Soroban-serializable type — built-ins like `Symbol`, `u32`, `Address`, or your own `#[contracttype]` structs and enums — with the XDR-encoded key capped at **250 bytes** and the value at **64 KiB**. Every transaction must declare up front, in its _footprint_, exactly which entries it will read and write. And every entry pays **rent**: it has a TTL (time-to-live, in ledgers) that only moves when someone explicitly extends it, and rent is charged when you write or extend. When the TTL runs out, persistent and instance entries are archived; temporary entries are deleted forever.

That model has three consequences that drive everything below:

- **You cannot iterate what you cannot name.** There is no "give me all keys starting with X". To enumerate, you build the index yourself.

- **Every entry you touch costs budget.** Reads, writes, and bytes are metered per transaction and capped per ledger. A design that touches 300 entries in one call simply does not execute.

- **State is not free forever.** Every byte kept alive has a recurring cost, and every entry needs a TTL story.

### The three storage tiers

`env.storage()` gives you three APIs with the same interface but different _lifecycles_. Watch what happens to each tier's entry when its TTL runs out:

<StorageDiagram n={0} />

|  | **instance()** | **persistent()** | **temporary()** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lives in | the contract instance's own entry | its own entry per key | its own entry per key |
| On TTL expiry | archived together with the contract (they share one entry) | archived — auto-restored on next use (rent re-paid) | **deleted forever** |
| Rent | shared with the instance | full rate | **half** rate |
| Loaded when | **every invocation** | only when in the footprint | only when in the footprint |
| Right for | small, global, contract-lifetime config | data you must never lose | data with a natural deadline, or safely regenerable |

Four subtleties that bite newcomers:

- **Nothing extends a TTL automatically.** The host never bumps a TTL on access — on any tier. Every extension is an explicit `extend_ttl()` call by the contract (or a transaction operation). What looks automatic in well-run contracts is the bump-on-access pattern (Strategy 5), applied to instance and persistent entries alike.

- **Instance storage is one single entry.** Everything in it is deserialized on every call and shares the 64 KiB cap. And since protocol 23 executes non-conflicting transactions in parallel, two transactions that both write instance data cannot run concurrently. Keep it small and mostly read-only.

- **Temporary is not "scratch space".** It is durable across transactions until its TTL runs out — but expiry _permanently deletes_ it: no archive, no recovery. Use it only for data whose loss is acceptable or whose validity provably ends at a known ledger. In exchange it rents at half price and never needs restoring.

- **Persistent entries don't disappear — they archive.** Since protocol 23, an archived entry is **restored automatically** when a transaction declares it in the read-write footprint — that transaction re-pays the storage rent plus disk-read fees (simulation builds the footprint; the explicit `RestoreFootprint` operation still exists but is rarely needed).

### The limits (Mainnet, protocol 27, verified live 2026-07-16)

Fetched live via `stellar network settings` — the same data [lab.stellar.org/network-limits](https://lab.stellar.org/network-limits) renders. Validators vote on these; always check current values.

| Per transaction | Limit | Practical meaning |
| --- | --: | --- |
| CPU instructions | 400,000,000 | compute budget for the whole invocation tree |
| Memory | 40 MiB | host + guest memory |
| **Footprint entries** (read + write) | **400** | max distinct entries one transaction may touch |
| Disk-read entries / bytes | 200 / 200,000 | archived & classic entries only — live Soroban state is served from memory since protocol 23 |
| **Written entries / bytes** | **200** / 132,096 | distinct entries written; sum of written entry sizes (~129 KiB) |
| Transaction size | 132,096 B | envelope incl. footprint — big footprints eat your payload |
| Events + return value | 16,384 B | total emitted event size |

| Per ledger (~5 s)         |           Limit |
| ------------------------- | --------------: |
| CPU instructions          |     580,000,000 |
| Disk read entries / bytes | 1,000 / 400,000 |
| Write entries / bytes     | 1,000 / 286,720 |
| Soroban transactions      |           2,000 |

| Sizes & TTLs (static)           |                     Value |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------: |
| Max ledger key size             |                     250 B |
| Max data entry size             |         65,536 B (64 KiB) |
| **Max entry TTL**               | 3,110,400 ledgers ≈ 180 d |
| Min TTL: persistent / temporary |           ≈ 120 d / ≈ 1 d |

:::note

Two numbers to burn into memory: **`17,280` = one day of ledgers** (at the network's 5 s _target_ close time — observed ledgers average slightly longer, so day-based TTLs err on the generous side; nearly every production codebase defines `DAY_IN_LEDGERS` and expresses TTLs in days), and **64 KiB per entry** — any collection kept inside a single entry has a hard ceiling, and a soft ceiling far below it, because big entries make every read and write expensive.

:::

{/* section:s1 */}

## Strategy 1: Singleton config in instance storage

_instance · O(1) · zero extra reads_

**You need.** A handful of values every call uses: admin address, token addresses, a pause flag, pool reserves, a counter.

**The catch.** These values are read on virtually every invocation. If each lived in its own persistent entry, every call would pay reads for each one and you'd manage several TTLs. But the contract instance entry is _already_ loaded on every call — data stored inside it costs no extra reads.

<StorageDiagram n={1} />

**The pattern.** Put them in `instance()` storage under unit-like enum keys, and extend the instance TTL as part of normal operation:

```rust
#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey { Admin, Token0, Token1, Reserve0, Reserve1 }

pub fn __constructor(e: Env, admin: Address) {
    e.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin);
}

// every public function starts with:
e.storage().instance().extend_ttl(INSTANCE_LIFETIME_THRESHOLD, INSTANCE_BUMP_AMOUNT);
```

**Trade-offs**

- O(1), zero extra footprint entries — the cheapest storage you'll ever use.

- Everything in it is deserialized on every call and shares the 64 KiB cap. A signer set of 10 keys is fine; a map of 10,000 users is a bug.

- Instance writes serialize concurrent transactions. Hot mutable data with many independent writers (per-user balances) does **not** belong here — AMM reserves are acceptable because every swap conflicts logically anyway.

**In the wild**

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — nearly every example: `increment`, `single_offer` (whole `Offer` struct), `liquidity_pool` (tokens, reserves, shares), `account` (signer set).

- `soroswap/core` — `pair/src/storage.rs` keeps `Token0/Token1/Reserve0/Reserve1/Factory/KLast` in instance storage: every swap touches reserves, so co-locating them minimizes footprint.

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — `pool/src/storage.rs`: admin, backstop, config under `Symbol` keys.

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — token metadata, `Paused` flag, `Owner`/`PendingOwner`.

{/* section:s2 */}

## Strategy 2: One entry per entity — the `DataKey` enum map

_persistent · O(1) lookup · max parallelism · no enumeration_

**You need.** Per-user (or per-asset, per-order, per-anything) state: balances, positions, configs. Unbounded population.

**The catch.** A naive `Map<Address, i128>` under one key hits three walls at once: the 64 KiB entry cap (~1,000 address→i128 pairs and you're done), the write-bytes budget (every update rewrites the whole map), and parallel-execution contention (every user's transaction conflicts with every other's).

<StorageDiagram n={2} />

**The pattern.** Give every entity its own ledger entry, using an enum variant with a parameter as the key. This is Soroban's equivalent of Solidity's `mapping`:

```rust
#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey {
    Balance(Address),      // one persistent entry per holder
}

pub fn read_balance(e: &Env, addr: Address) -> i128 {
    let key = DataKey::Balance(addr);
    if let Some(balance) = e.storage().persistent().get::<_, i128>(&key) {
        e.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, BALANCE_LIFETIME_THRESHOLD, BALANCE_BUMP_AMOUNT);
        balance
    } else {
        0   // absent entry == zero; never write zeros you don't need
    }
}
```

Note the two idioms: **absent-means-default** (don't create entries to store zero) and **bump-on-access** (Strategy 5).

**Trade-offs**

- O(1) lookup and update; transactions that touch different users' entries never conflict → maximal parallelism, minimal footprint.

- You lose enumeration entirely — there is no way to list all `Balance(..)` keys on-chain. If you need "all holders", add an index (Strategy 8) or index events off-chain.

- Aggregate rent grows with users — but each user's activity pays for that user's own entries, which puts the cost exactly where the benefit is.

**In the wild.** The single most common pattern on Soroban — the survey found it in essentially every non-trivial contract:

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `token/src/balance.rs`, `liquidity_pool` (`Shares(Address)`).

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — fungible `Balance(Address)`; NFT `Owner(u32)` — one entry per token.

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — `Contracts(Address) → bool` deployment registry.

- `kalepail/passkey-kit` — per-signer entries in each smart wallet.

{/* section:s3 */}

## Strategy 3: Composite keys — multi-dimensional lookups

_persistent · temporary · O(1) · key ≤ 250 B_

**You need.** State indexed by _two or more_ dimensions: allowance of `(owner, spender)`, position of `(pool, user)`, mint quota of `(contract, minter, epoch)`.

**The catch.** Same as Strategy 2 — nested maps in one entry don't scale — plus a new constraint: the **250-byte key cap**. A key is itself an XDR-serialized value; two addresses plus a few integers fit easily, but never put unbounded strings or vectors in a key.

<StorageDiagram n={3} />

**The pattern.** Put a struct (or tuple variant) inside the key:

```rust
#[contracttype]
pub struct AllowanceDataKey { pub from: Address, pub spender: Address }

#[contracttype]
pub enum DataKey { Allowance(AllowanceDataKey) }
```

A powerful refinement: put a **time bucket in the key** to get self-partitioning data. The mint-lock example keys per-epoch consumption as `MinterStats(contract, minter, epoch_length, epoch)` — a new epoch simply _starts writing a different key_, and old epochs expire on their own (Strategy 4):

```rust
let epoch = e.ledger().sequence() / config.epoch_length;
let key = StorageKey::MinterStats(contract, minter, config.epoch_length, epoch);
```

**Trade-offs**

- Still O(1) per lookup; each combination is an independent entry — parallelism preserved.

- Key design is API design: you can only look up by the _exact_ full key. If you also need "all spenders for an owner", that's an enumeration problem (Strategy 8).

- More dimensions = more entries; fine, as long as each is paid for by whoever benefits from it.

**In the wild**

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `token/src/allowance.rs` (`(from, spender)`), `mint-lock` (epoch-bucketed minter stats).

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — `UserBalance(PoolUserKey{pool,user})`, `UserEmis(UserReserveKey{user,reserve_id})`, auctions keyed `(auction_type, user)`.

- `soroswap/core` — `PairAddressesByTokens(Pair)` with the sorted token tuple → O(1) pair lookup.

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — `ApprovalForAll(Address, Address)`, `HasRole(Address, Symbol)`.

{/* section:s4 */}

## Strategy 4: Temporary storage for data with a deadline

_temporary · half rent · auto-GC_

**You need.** State that is only meaningful until some ledger: allowances with expiry, live auctions, oracle prices, per-epoch quotas, pending admin proposals.

**The catch.** Rent. Park ephemeral data in persistent storage and you pay full-rate rent _and_ carry dead entries forever — there's no built-in "delete after X", and cleanup writes cost budget too.

<StorageDiagram n={4} />

**The pattern.** Use `temporary()` storage and make the TTL _be_ the business logic — set it to expire exactly when the data stops being valid:

```rust
// SEP-41 token allowance (SEP-41 is Soroban's standard token interface)
e.storage().temporary().set(&key, &AllowanceValue { amount, expiration_ledger });
if amount > 0 {
    let live_for = expiration_ledger.checked_sub(e.ledger().sequence()).unwrap();
    e.storage().temporary().extend_ttl(&key, live_for, live_for);
}
```

The TTL alone is not the whole guarantee, for two reasons: the network enforces a **1-day minimum** TTL (a deadline closer than 17,280 ledgers leaves the entry alive past it), and anyone can extend any entry's TTL with an `ExtendFootprintTTLOp`. So defensive code **also stores the deadline in the value and checks it** — as above, `expiration_ledger` lives inside `AllowanceValue`. The network guarantees deletion once the TTL runs out; your code enforces validity until then.

**Trade-offs**

- Half-price rent, automatic garbage collection, zero cleanup transactions.

- Deleted means deleted — never put funds-bearing or must-not-lose state here. If nobody extends the entry and it expires early, your code must treat "absent" identically to "expired".

- Minimum TTL is 1 day — sub-day deadlines must be enforced by the value check, not the TTL.

**In the wild**

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `token/src/allowance.rs`, the canonical example; `mint-lock` epoch stats extended exactly to end-of-epoch.

- `reflector-network/reflector-contract` — the timestamp-keyed price history above (`oracle/src/prices.rs`); same shape in `script3/sep-40-oracle`, `diadata-org/soroban-oracles`, `bandprotocol/band-std-reference-contracts-soroban`.

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — auctions, queued reserve configs (auto-expiring admin timelock), and `ProposedAdmin` with a 10-day TTL: an admin handover offer that rescinds itself.

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — NFT approvals and fungible allowances, all temporary with `live_until_ledger` in the value.

{/* section:s5 */}

## Strategy 5: TTL management — bump-on-access

_persistent · instance · rent tracks usage_

**You need.** Persistent data that must not archive while in use — without paying maximum rent on everything forever.

**The catch.** Every persistent entry archives when its TTL hits zero, and the next transaction to touch an archived entry pays restoration rent and disk-read fees on top of its own (auto-restore, protocol 23+). But extending a TTL costs rent proportional to entry size × ledgers added, so bumping everything to max on every touch is wasteful — and _never_ bumping guarantees eventual archival. Max TTL is ~180 days; you cannot "set and forget".

<StorageDiagram n={5} />

**The pattern.** The ecosystem has converged on a pair of constants and a rule — _if fewer than `THRESHOLD` ledgers remain, extend to `BUMP`_ — applied on every read and write:

```rust
pub(crate) const DAY_IN_LEDGERS: u32 = 17280;
pub(crate) const BALANCE_BUMP_AMOUNT: u32 = 30 * DAY_IN_LEDGERS;                    // extend to 30 days
pub(crate) const BALANCE_LIFETIME_THRESHOLD: u32 = BALANCE_BUMP_AMOUNT - DAY_IN_LEDGERS; // when < 29 days left

e.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, BALANCE_LIFETIME_THRESHOLD, BALANCE_BUMP_AMOUNT);
```

`extend_ttl(threshold, bump)` only acts when fewer than `threshold` ledgers remain — otherwise it's a no-op. So `THRESHOLD = BUMP − 1 day` means an active entry gets at most one small extension per day, and rent cost tracks actual usage. Real-world constants, from the survey:

| Codebase | Data class | Threshold → Bump |
| --- | --- | --: |
| `stellar/soroban-examples` token | instance / balances | 6 → 7 d / 29 → 30 d |
| `soroswap/core` | instance / pair registry / LP balances | 29 → 30 / 59 → 60 / 119 → 120 d |
| `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` | instance / shared protocol / user data | 30 → 31 / 45 → 46 / **100 → 120 d** |

Note the deliberate gradient: the more user-owned and loss-painful the data, the longer the bump. Blend's user positions get 120 days (near the ~180-day max) because an archived position is a support incident; shared reserve data gets 46 because _any_ user's transaction re-bumps it constantly.

**Trade-offs**

- Bump-on-access means rent is paid by the people using the data, exactly when they use it. Idle data eventually archives — the _intended_ economics, not a failure.

- It cannot keep alive what nobody touches. For "must survive total inactivity" data you need an off-chain keeper calling `ExtendFootprintTTLOp` periodically, or you accept auto-restore-on-return (the returning transaction re-pays the rent).

- Getters that bump TTL are technically metadata writes; cheap, but simulation vs. submission footprints can differ — the SDK handles it, just don't be surprised.

**In the wild.** Universal — this appeared in more surveyed files than any other single pattern: the token example's `balance.rs`, every OpenZeppelin storage module (per-package `*_TTL_THRESHOLD`/`*_EXTEND_AMOUNT` constants), Blend's `get_persistent_default()` helper bundling get + default + bump, Soroswap's `get_persistent_extend_or_error()`, and `FredericRezeau/soroban-kit`, which wraps the whole idiom in macros.

{/* section:s6 */}

## Strategy 6: Bounded collections in a single entry

_persistent · 1 read to iterate · hard cap in code_

**You need.** A small list the _whole contract_ shares and iterates: the assets a lending pool supports, a reward-zone registry, a withdrawal queue.

**The catch.** Iterating N separate entries costs N footprint reads (cap: 400 per transaction, each one billed). But an unbounded `Vec` in one entry eventually hits 64 KiB — and every writer of the list conflicts with every other.

<StorageDiagram n={6} />

**The pattern.** Keep the collection in one entry **and enforce a hard cap in code**, chosen so the entry stays small and iteration stays cheap:

```rust
pub const MAX_RESERVES: u32 = 30;   // blend pool/src/constants.rs

pub fn push_res_list(e: &Env, asset: &Address) -> u32 {
    let mut res_list = get_res_list(e);
    if res_list.len() >= MAX_RESERVES {
        panic_with_error!(e, PoolError::BadRequest)
    }
    let new_index = res_list.len();
    res_list.push_back(asset.clone());
    e.storage().persistent().set(&Symbol::new(e, RES_LIST_KEY), &res_list);
    // + extend_ttl
    new_index
}
```

The list entry stores only _identifiers_; per-item detail lives in its own entry (Strategy 2/3). Reading "the whole configuration" is then 1 + N reads where N ≤ cap.

**Trade-offs**

- One read fetches the whole list → O(n) in-memory iteration, no footprint explosion. Append is O(1).

- The cap is a **product decision** disguised as an engineering one: Blend pools can never exceed 30 reserves. Pick caps deliberately (entry bytes ≈ n × item size; 30 addresses ≈ 1.2 KiB — comfortable).

- Single-entry writes serialize; fine for admin-touched lists, wrong for user-touched ones.

- Removal is O(n) — later items shift down one slot. Acceptable at n ≤ 30; for O(1) removal use swap-and-pop (Strategy 8).

**In the wild**

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — the flagship user: reserve list capped at 30, reward zone capped at 30 (with evict-to-insert logic), per-user withdrawal queue `Vec<Q4W>` capped at 20 _inside_ the user-balance entry.

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `timelock` stores `claimants: Vec<Address>` (implicitly small) inside one struct.

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — `ExistingRoles: Vec<Symbol>` with a `MAX_ROLES` guard.

{/* section:s7 */}

## Strategy 7: Pack vs. split — sizing the entry to the transaction

_persistent · group by usage_

**You need.** An entity with several related pieces of state — say a user's collateral, debt, and supplied assets — and a decision: one entry holding all of it, or one entry per piece?

**The catch.** This is a genuine two-sided trap. **Split too much** and a single operation burns many footprint entries — a health check needing a user's 10 positions as 10 entries pays 10 reads plus more for each reserve's config, edging toward the 400-entry cap. **Pack too much** and you re-serialize a big blob on every small change (write-bytes fees), edge toward 64 KiB, and lose write parallelism between independent updates.

<StorageDiagram n={7} />

**The pattern.** Group by how transactions use the data: pieces that are always read and written **together, atomically** belong in one entry; pieces updated independently (or by different actors) belong apart.

Blend's `Positions` entry is the canonical "pack" example — every borrow, repay, and liquidation must see _all_ of a user's positions to check account health, so they share one entry:

```rust
#[contracttype]
pub struct Positions {                       // ONE persistent entry per user
    pub liabilities: Map<u32, i128>,         // reserve_index -> dTokens
    pub collateral: Map<u32, i128>,
    pub supply: Map<u32, i128>,
}
```

Bounded by the pool's `max_positions` config — Strategy 6 applied _inside_ an entry. Note the maps key by reserve index (`u32`), not `Address`: smaller entry, cross-referencing the Strategy 6 reserve list. Meanwhile Blend's reserves are _split_ — `ResConfig` vs `ResData` per asset — because config changes are rare admin ops while rates change on every interaction; packing them would rewrite config bytes on every rate update.

**Trade-offs**

|  | Packed (1 entry) | Split (n entries) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read whole entity | 1 read | n reads |
| Update one field | rewrite whole blob | 1 small write |
| Atomicity | free | you maintain invariants across entries |
| Parallelism between parts | none | full |
| Size ceiling | 64 KiB for everything | 64 KiB per part |

**In the wild**

- Packed: Blend `Positions` and backstop `UserBalance { shares, q4w }`; OpenZeppelin's smart-account `ContextRuleEntry` bundling rule metadata + signer ids + policy ids — cutting every auth check from 3 reads to 1; the timelock example's whole `ClaimableBalance` struct.

- Split: Blend `ResConfig`/`ResData` pairs; OZ fungible `Balance` vs `Allowance` vs `Meta`; every token's balance-per-entry layout.

{/* section:s8 */}

## Strategy 8: Enumeration — indexes you maintain yourself

_persistent · O(1) maintain · pageable reads_

**You need.** To _list_ things on-chain: all trading pairs a factory created, all tokens an address owns, all members of a role. (Strategy 2 deliberately gave this up.)

**The catch.** No key iteration exists, unbounded Vecs are forbidden by the 64 KiB cap, and any O(n)-rewrite maintenance would eventually exceed per-transaction budgets. You need an index that is O(1) to _maintain_ and pageable to _read_.

<StorageDiagram n={8} />

**The pattern — three variants by mutability.** **(a) Append-only: counter + indexed keys.** For sets that only grow, store `Total` and one entry per index:

```rust
// soroswap factory
enum DataKey {
    TotalPairs,                    // instance: u32
    PairAddressesNIndexed(u32),    // persistent: index -> pair address
    PairAddressesByTokens(Pair),   // persistent: (tokenA,tokenB) -> pair address
}
```

Appending = write index `n`, bump counter. Enumeration = clients loop `all_pairs(i)` for `i in 0..total` — **pagination is pushed to the caller**, which is the point: no single transaction ever needs the whole set. Note Soroswap maintains _two_ indexes over the same data — direct lookup by tokens _and_ positional enumeration.

**(b) Mutable set: double mapping + swap-and-pop.** When items can also be _removed_, maintain two mappings — forward (`index → item`) and reverse (`item → index`) — so removal is O(1), as animated above:

```rust
// OpenZeppelin enumerable NFT, abridged
if to_be_removed_index != last_token_index {
    let last_token_id = get_owner_token_id(e, owner, last_token_index);
    set(OwnerTokens(owner, to_be_removed_index), last_token_id);   // move last into hole
    set(OwnerTokensIndex(last_token_id), to_be_removed_index);     // fix reverse pointer
}
remove(OwnerTokens(owner, last_token_index));                      // pop tail
```

**(c) Zero on-chain index: events + off-chain indexer.** If only off-chain consumers need the listing, emit events and let an indexer (RPC `getEvents`, Hubble, etc.) build the list. On-chain cost: zero entries. On-chain readability: none.

**Trade-offs**

| Variant | add | remove | contains | on-chain page read | keeps order |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (a) counter + index | O(1) | ✗ (or tombstone) | via 2nd index | O(page) | yes |
| (b) double map + swap-pop | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | O(page) | no |
| (c) events only | O(1) | O(1) | ✗ | ✗ | n/a |

In the double-map variant, each indexed item costs 2 entries (forward + reverse) of rent — roughly 2× the storage of Strategy 2; variant (a) adds ~1 per item. Add an index only where the _contract itself_ needs the list.

**In the wild**

- (a) `soroswap/core` factory — the dual-index registry.

- (b) `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — three independent uses, same shape: enumerable NFTs, access-control role members, fee-abstraction allowlist. Three occurrences inside one standard library is the strongest "this is _the_ idiom" signal in the whole survey.

- (c) implicit in most protocols: Blend emits events for auctions/positions and exposes no "list all users" — off-chain indexers own it.

{/* section:s9 */}

## Strategy 9: Two-level indexes — O(1) accounting for unbounded populations

_persistent · O(1) per user · never iterate_

**You need.** To distribute something (interest, rewards, emissions) _continuously_ to an unbounded set of holders — without ever touching more than one holder per transaction.

**The catch.** The naive design — loop over holders and update each — is impossible on Soroban not just in fees but in _footprint_: you cannot write 10,000 entries, ever, in any transaction (200-write cap). The design must be O(1) per user by construction.

<StorageDiagram n={9} />

**The pattern.** The index/snapshot pattern (DeFi folklore calls it "MasterChef", after the SushiSwap staking contract that popularized it): one _global_ entry per pool plus one _snapshot_ entry per user:

```rust
#[contracttype]
pub struct ReserveEmissionData {   // ONE entry per reserve
    pub index: i128,               // cumulative rewards-per-share; only ever increases
    pub eps: u64, pub expiration: u64, pub last_time: u64,
}
#[contracttype]
pub struct UserEmissionData {      // ONE entry per (user, reserve)
    pub index: i128,               // the global index last time this user was touched
    pub accrued: i128,
}
// on any user action:  accrued += user_shares * (global.index - user.index);
//                      user.index = global.index;
```

Time advances the _global_ index lazily; each user settles the delta since _their own_ last touch, whenever they show up. Nobody ever iterates.

**Trade-offs**

- O(1) entries touched per user action — the only pattern that scales distribution to any population under Soroban's write caps.

- The math must be exactly right (rounding, index monotonicity); this is the highest-audit-risk pattern in this handbook.

- Users who never interact never settle — fine for rewards (they accrue by formula), but the pattern cannot push _obligations_ to passive users.

- TTL pairing: Blend gives the global entry 45 → 46 days (re-bumped constantly, by everyone) and user snapshots 100 → 120 days (only that user bumps them). TTL gradients follow access patterns.

**In the wild**

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — twice, independently: pool emissions and backstop emissions; interest itself uses the same idea via `b_rate`/`d_rate` cumulative rates.

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — checkpointed voting power (`fungible/extensions/votes`) is the same lazy-accounting family, with binary-searched historical checkpoints.

- `Phoenix-Protocol-Group/phoenix-contracts` — stake `distribution.rs`, the same two-level reward index.

{/* section:s10 */}

## Strategy 10: Don't store it at all

_derived keys · sentinel values · commitments_

**You need.** To handle large or numerous records — proposals, scheduled operations, airdrop entitlements — whose full contents would be expensive or impossible to keep on-chain.

**The catch.** Every stored byte is rent forever (or TTL babysitting); every entry is footprint. The cheapest entry is the one that doesn't exist.

<StorageDiagram n={10} />

**The pattern — three escalating tricks.** **(a) Deterministic IDs.** Never store what can be _recomputed_. OpenZeppelin's Governor doesn't store proposal contents at all — the proposal ID is _derived by hashing_ the contents; at execution, callers re-supply the contents and the contract re-hashes to verify:

```rust
// governor: proposal_id = keccak256(xdr(targets, functions, args, description_hash))
// timelock: operation_id = keccak256(xdr(target, fn, args, predecessor, salt))
```

**(b) Sentinel-value state machines.** OZ's Timelock stores a _single_ `u32` per operation — a scheduled timestamp — and encodes the whole lifecycle in it: `0` = unset, `1` = done, `timestamp > now` = waiting, `timestamp ≤ now` = ready. Blend's auctions similarly derive "stale" from the auction's block age instead of storing a status field. Derived state can't go stale and costs zero extra bytes.

**(c) Commitments to off-chain data.** For big datasets, store only a cryptographic commitment; users bring the data + proof. The Merkle airdrop keeps **one** 32-byte root for an arbitrarily large distribution list, plus one `Claimed(index)` flag per _actual_ claimer:

```rust
enum DataKey { RootHash, TokenAddress, Claimed(u32) }
// claim(index, receiver, amount, proof) -> verify proof against RootHash, set Claimed(index)
```

**Trade-offs**

- (a)/(b): nearly zero on-chain cost; the price is API ergonomics — callers must re-provide inputs, and clients must be able to reconstruct them (events help).

- (c): shifts data availability off-chain — someone must host the Merkle tree, and a lost tree means unclaimable entitlements. Proof verification is cheap CPU-wise: O(log n) hashes.

- Lazy-write is the same philosophy applied to writes: OZ Governor creates vote-tally entries only on the _first_ vote and computes proposal states (Pending/Active/Succeeded) from `ProposalCore` + clock — don't write what you can derive.

**In the wild**

- `OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts` — Governor + Timelock, Merkle distributor.

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `merkle_distribution`.

- `kalepail/passkey-kit` — verifies WebAuthn passkey signatures per call rather than storing session state.

{/* section:s11 */}

## Strategy 11: Scale out — contract-per-entity via factory

_instance ×N · isolation · horizontal scale_

**You need.** Effectively unlimited growth — a DEX with thousands of markets, a wallet per user, a pool per risk profile — beyond what any single contract's storage design can comfortably hold.

**The catch.** Even with perfect per-entry layout, one contract concentrates everything: one instance entry every transaction must load (contention), one 64 KiB instance ceiling, one blast radius for bugs and upgrades, and per-ledger read/write caps shared by _all_ users of the contract.

<StorageDiagram n={11} />

**The pattern.** Deploy a **contract per entity** from a factory, and keep only the registry in the factory (Strategy 8 for the index, Strategy 2 for the reverse lookup). Each pair/pool/wallet gets its own instance storage, its own TTLs, its own parallelism domain:

```rust
// soroswap factory: deterministic deployment + dual registry
let pair_address = create_contract(&e, pair_wasm_hash, &token_pair); // deploys pair contract
put_pair_address_by_token_pair(&e, token_pair, &pair_address);      // (tokenA,tokenB) -> addr
add_pair_to_all_pairs(&e, &pair_address);                           // index n -> addr
```

The factory records `is_deployed`-style flags so other contracts can verify provenance.

**Trade-offs**

- Horizontal scale and isolation: pair A's storage never contends with pair B's; each entity's instance data enjoys Strategy 1 economics locally.

- Cross-entity operations become cross-contract calls (CPU + footprint per hop); a router contract usually papers over this — Soroswap's router holds exactly one storage key: the factory address.

- Fleet upgrades are real operational work (N contracts to upgrade), and each instance needs its own TTL liveness.

**In the wild**

- `soroswap/core` — factory + pair + router, the full Uniswap-v2 topology.

- `blend-capital/blend-contracts-v2` — `pool-factory` deploys isolated lending pools; the backstop then keys its own state by pool address (Strategy 3).

- `kalepail/passkey-kit` — one smart-wallet contract per user, deployed on passkey registration.

- `stellar/soroban-examples` — `deployer` shows the primitive.

{/* section:longtail */}

## From the survey's long tail

Three patterns appeared too rarely to earn a full strategy, but are worth recognizing:

- **Lazy schema migration.** Contracts are upgradeable, but their storage entries keep the old layout. Store a version number alongside the data; on read, apply registered transforms to migrate stale entries to the current schema — no downtime, no mass-migration transactions. Seen in `Stellar-Teye/Teye-Contracts` (`lazy_read` + per-version transforms) and `Templar-Protocol/contracts` (version-tagged decode, one decoder per schema version).

- **Tier-abstraction traits.** `allbridge-public/allbridge-core-soroban-contracts` wraps get/set/extend_ttl behind a `SorobanData` trait parameterized by storage tier, so each type declares its tier once. Nice ergonomics for a multi-contract codebase; same semantics underneath.

- **Blob paging (anti-pattern).** Splitting >64 KiB data into fixed-size page entries plus a manifest. It works, but every access pays per-page reads and writes — redesign toward bounded entries (S6), packing by cohesion (S7), or contract-per-entity (S11) before reaching for pages.

{/* section:path */}

## Choosing: a decision path

For each piece of state, walk this list:

1. **Can you avoid storing it?** Derivable → recompute. Large + user-provable → commitment. Only off-chain readers → events. **→ S10**

2. **Small, global, read by ~every call?** Instance storage; keep it under a few KiB. **→ S1**

3. **Validity ends at a known ledger, or loss is acceptable?** Temporary; TTL = deadline; deadline also in the value. **→ S4**

4. **Per-entity, unbounded population?** Persistent entry per entity; composite keys for extra dimensions; bump-on-access TTLs. **→ S2 · S3 · S5**

5. **Several pieces update atomically together?** Pack into one bounded entry. Updated independently or by different actors? Split. **→ S7**

6. **The contract must iterate it?** Small & admin-managed → bounded Vec in one entry. Large or user-managed → counter/index entries; add reverse map + swap-and-pop if removable. **→ S6 · S8**

7. **Distributing value over the population?** Two-level index; never iterate. **→ S9**

8. **Still too big or too contended?** Shard into contract-per-entity via factory. **→ S11**

{/* section:cheat */}

## Cheatsheet

### Tier picker

| Data | Tier | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admin, config, token metadata, pause flag | instance | loaded every call anyway; one entry |
| AMM reserves / totals (every swap updates them anyway) | instance | co-located with instance; the write conflict is inherent to the product |
| Balances, ownership, positions, long-lived registries | persistent | must never be lost; archive + restore safety net |
| Allowances, approvals, auctions, epoch stats, pending proposals | temporary | natural deadline; half rent; auto-GC |
| Oracle prices / regenerable caches | temporary | loss is cheap, freshness is the point |
| Anything derivable (states, IDs, tallies pre-first-vote) | _none_ | recompute; hash-commit; lazy-create |

### Mainnet numbers to memorize (2026-07 — check lab.stellar.org)

```text
1 day  = 17,280 ledgers (5s)          max entry TTL   = 3,110,400 (~180 d)
entry  ≤ 64 KiB   key ≤ 250 B         min persistent TTL ≈ 120 d, min temp ≈ 1 d
per tx : 400 footprint entries, 200 writes / 129 KiB, 200 disk reads / 195 KiB,
         400M instr, 40 MiB mem, 129 KiB tx size, 16 KiB events
per 5s ledger: 1,000 writes / 280 KiB, 2,000 soroban txs, 580M instr
temporary rent ≈ ½ persistent rent
```

### The TTL recipe

```rust
const DAY_IN_LEDGERS: u32 = 17280;
const BUMP: u32      = 30 * DAY_IN_LEDGERS;   // pick per data class, see gradient below
const THRESHOLD: u32 = BUMP - DAY_IN_LEDGERS; // re-bump at most ~daily
// on every read AND write of the entry:
storage.extend_ttl(&key, THRESHOLD, BUMP);
```

Gradient observed in production: **instance 7–31 d** · **shared/protocol 45–60 d · user-owned 100–120 d** · **temporary = exact deadline**. Longer = more loss-painful, less frequently re-touched.

### Pattern → complexity

| Pattern | Lookup | Insert | Remove | Enumerate | Entries/item | § |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instance singleton | O(1)\* | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | 0 (shared) | S1 |
| Entry per entity | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | ✗ | 1 | S2/S3 |
| Bounded Vec in one entry | O(n) in-mem | O(1) | O(n) | O(n), 1 read | 1/n | S6 |
| Packed struct per entity | O(1) whole | rewrite blob | O(1) | ✗ | 1 | S7 |
| Counter + index entries | O(1) by idx | O(1) | ✗ | O(page) | 1 | S8a |
| Double map + swap-and-pop | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | O(page), unordered | 2 | S8b |
| Two-level reward index | O(1)/user | — | — | ✗ | 1 + 1/user | S9 |
| Merkle commitment | O(log n) verify | root update | ✗ | ✗ | 1/claimer | S10c |
| Factory / contract-per-entity | O(1) + xcall | deploy | — | via registry | own contract | S11 |

\* loaded with every invocation regardless. "Entries/item": 1/n = one shared entry holds all n items; 2 = forward + reverse index entries; 1 + 1/user = one global entry plus one per user.

### Red flags in review

- `Map<Address, _>` or unbounded `Vec` under a single key → will hit 64 KiB; use S2/S8.

- Funds-critical data in `temporary()` → unrecoverable after expiry.

- Persistent writes with no `extend_ttl` anywhere → entries archive when the minimum ~120-day TTL runs out; users' next txs then pay restoration rent on top of their own fees.

- Loop over "all users" on-chain → impossible at scale (200-write cap); use S9.

- Mutable hot data in `instance()` with many independent writers → parallel-execution contention; move to per-entity entries.

- TTL as the _only_ expiry check on temporary data → also store the deadline in the value and check it (S4).

- Data paged across entries because it outgrew 64 KiB → redesign (bound it, split by cohesion, or shard by contract) rather than page.

{/* section:survey */}

## Survey: who uses what

Produced with a GitHub code-search crawl across public Rust repos importing `soroban_sdk`, anchored on tier accessors, `extend_ttl`, `DataKey` enums, and TTL constants. The crawl kept **874 contract files across 493 public repositories** (only files scored medium-or-higher confidence; SDK-internal files down-ranked). Survey date: 2026-07-09.

| Pattern                            | Repos | Share | Strategy |
| ---------------------------------- | ----: | ----: | -------- |
| Persistent per-entity storage      |   374 |   76% | S2       |
| Explicit TTL management            |   354 |   72% | S5       |
| Composite keys                     |   345 |   70% | S3       |
| Instance storage for config        |   341 |   69% | S1       |
| Temporary storage                  |   220 |   45% | S4       |
| `DataKey`/`StorageKey` enum layout |   211 |   43% | S2       |
| Expiry semantics in values         |   156 |   32% | S4       |
| Pagination / index entries         |    67 |   14% | S8       |
| Bucketing / chunking               |     9 |    2% | S6/S10   |

Reading: the tier system + keyed-enum layout + bump-on-access TTLs are **table stakes** — nearly every real contract does all three, almost always copied from the SEP-41 token example's `balance.rs`/`allowance.rs` shape. Enumeration indexes appear only where a product actually lists things on-chain (~1 in 7 repos). Bucketing is exotic.

_Caveats: GitHub code search pages are capped, so this is a sample, not a census; category counts are slightly inflated by the `extend_ttl` query anchor; forks counted separately._
